sections.title: 1.1 Background
sections.text:
The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs), capacitor banks
(CBs), and electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs) in modern power distribution systems
Energies 2026, 19, 3262 https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143262
Energies 2026, 19, 3262 2 of 23
is driven by the global transition toward sustainable and low-carbon energy infrastruc-
tures. This transition directly supports several Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),
particularly SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infras-
tructure), and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) [1,2]. Consequently, active
power distribution networks (APDNs) are evolving from passive energy delivery systems
into intelligent and flexible networks capable of integrating renewable energy resources
while maintaining reliable operation.
The integration of distributed generation (DG) units, CBs, and EVCSs offers significant
technical and environmental benefits, including improved energy efficiency, reduced green-
house gas emissions, enhanced voltage regulation, and increased system flexibility [3,4].
However, the rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) introduces new operational challenges
due to the substantial and often concentrated charging demand imposed on distribution
networks. High EV penetration levels can increase network loading, voltage deviations,
and power losses, making coordinated planning and operation essential [5,6].
To address these challenges, several studies have investigated the concept of hosting
factors (HFs), which quantify the capability of distribution networks to accommodate
additional DERs and EV charging demand. In particular, the EV hosting factor (EV_HF)
has been identified as a critical parameter influencing network performance, power losses,
and voltage profiles [7]. Previous research has demonstrated that incorporating EV_HF into
planning strategies can simultaneously reduce active power losses and improve voltage
regulation throughout the network [8].
Various optimization approaches have been proposed to determine the optimal allo-
cation and sizing of network components. For example, the Quantum-Behaved Gaussian
Mutational Dragonfly Algorithm (QGDA) was applied to solve complex planning prob-
lems in distribution systems [9], while Harmony Search and Particle Swarm Optimization
(PSO) techniques were employed to enhance voltage quality and overall network perfor-
mance [10]. Furthermore, the coordinated integration of distributed generators (DGs),
distributed static synchronous compensators (DSTATCOMs), and EVCSs has been shown
to improve system reliability and operational efficiency [11–13]. Other studies have focused
on minimizing electrical losses through the simultaneous placement of DGs and EVCSs
while considering hosting factor constraints [12,13].
Additional optimization methods, including Differential Evolution (DE), Grey Wolf
Optimizer (GWO), adaptive Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), and Fuzzy Analytic Hi-
erarchy Process (AHP), have been successfully utilized to minimize energy losses and
improve voltage profiles in distribution systems [14,15]. In some investigations, EV_HF
was assumed to be equivalent to the total load demand of the network [16], whereas other
studies concentrated on identifying optimal EVCS locations [17] or addressing EV charg-
ing uncertainties using probabilistic modeling approaches [18,19]. Moreover, integrating
renewable energy sources directly with EV charging stations has been reported to alleviate
network loading and enhance overall system performance [20].
Despite the considerable progress achieved in literature, most existing studies focus
on optimizing individual components or specific operational objectives. The coordinated
planning of DGs, CBs, and EVCSs while simultaneously considering network losses, volt-
age profile enhancement, and hosting factor constraints remains an active research area
requiring further investigation.

sections.title: 1.2 Difficulties in Contemporary Distribution Systems
sections.text:
Radial distribution systems continue to face several operational challenges despite
their widespread adoption. Due to their radial structure and unidirectional power flow
characteristics, these systems are particularly vulnerable to voltage drops, increased active
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143262
Energies 2026, 19, 3262 3 of 23
and reactive power losses, branch overloading, and reduced voltage stability margins.
The growing penetration of EVCSs further intensifies these issues because of the high and
concentrated charging demand associated with fast-charging facilities.
In addition, the intermittent nature of renewable-based DGs introduces uncertainty
in power generation, which can complicate network operation, protection coordination,
and power quality management. Without appropriate planning and control strategies,
the uncontrolled integration of EVCSs, DGs, and CBs may result in inefficient network
operation, increased operating costs, and reduced system reliability. Therefore, coordinated
optimization frameworks are essential to ensure secure, economical, and sustainable opera-
tion of modern distribution networks while supporting future growth in renewable energy
and electric vehicle adoption [21,22].

sections.title: 1.4 Contributions of Manuscript
sections.text:
This study depends on the CGO optimization methodology to include electric vehicle
charging stations (EVCS) under multiple hosting factors (30%, 40%, and 50%) while coordi-
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143262
Energies 2026, 19, 3262 4 of 23
nating the thermal capacity limits of distribution branches alongside the voltage profile
improvement and minimizing both the distribution power losses and the cost of energy
losses, while reducing the CO2 annual emissions. The work presented in this paper is based
on the Classification-based Global Optimization (CGO) framework for optimal DGs and
CBs placement. The extended framework fills a gap in the literature by addressing the
integrated planning of EVCSs, DGs, and CBs. The following are the main contributions of
this study:
1. The Optimization Scope: Incorporates EV charging stations under multiple hosting
factors into the existing CGO framework, enabling holistic planning of active and
reactive power resources alongside EV infrastructure.
2. Engineering-Driven Classification: Unlike purely algorithmic approaches, the pro-
posed method classifies network buses based on voltage sensitivity, active power
demand, and reactive power demand, ensuring optimization is guided by electrical
engineering principles.
3. Deterministic Optimization Framework: A structured global optimization function
is employed, eliminating randomness and parameter sensitivity associated with
metaheuristics while ensuring reproducible and interpretable solutions.
4. Superior Performance and Scalability: The method is validated on IEEE 33-bus and
69-bus systems, demonstrating significant improvements in loss reduction, voltage
stability, and computational efficiency compared to existing techniques under high
EV penetration.
5. Sustainability Alignment: By enhancing grid efficiency and facilitating renewable and
EV integration, the approach directly supports SDGs 7, 9, 11, and 13, contributing to
sustainable energy transition goals.
The mentioned existing methods in Table 1 are optimization techniques used for radial
distribution networks, but the work in this manuscript is done under the assumption of a
network having two EVCS, two CBs and two DGs; these operating conditions may not be
found for other existing algorithms, but the drawbacks of these existing methods are listed
in this table; the other tables in the manuscript show the obtained results of the proposed
approach, which is compared with the base case study but the operation with the proposed
approach is done with very high loading by addition of high EV penetration, although the
proposed approach verifies the optimal solution as compared with base case operation that
operates without any EV penetration.

sections.title: 2 Methodology
sections.text:
This section presents the proposed comprehensive planning methodology for optimal
allocation and sizing of EVCSs, DGs, and CBs in radial distribution networks. The method-
ology integrates three stages: (1) EVCS planning, (2) DG planning, and (3) CB planning.
Full-system evaluation including EVCSs, DGs, and CBs is implemented. The workflow
uses multi-objective optimization supported by power-flow calculations and branch-based
search strategies.

sections.title: 2.1 Overview of the Optimization Strategy
sections.text:
The algorithm begins with a base-case power flow analysis to capture the initial
operating conditions, including losses, voltage profile, and total load demand. The radial
network is decomposed into branches from the radial tree, each ranked according to:
1. Active power demand—for EVCS and DGs placement.
2. Reactive power demand—for CBs placement.
This classification ensures that resources are allocated to branches with the highest
need, improving search efficiency and solution quality. Firstly, EVCSs are optimally deter-
mined their placement and size based on the operating hosting factor, then DG units are
placed to address active power deficits, and finally CBs for reactive support. All placements
respect thermal limits, voltage constraints, and operational bounds.

VDI : voltage deviation index, CSaved Energy Loss is the annual saving due to reduced losses
($), ∆QCO2 is the annual CO2 emission reduction (kg/year), and W1, W2, W3, and W4 are
weighting factors. The weighting factors were selected based on normalized objective
functions and system priorities. Initially, equal weights were used, followed by tuning
through sensitivity analysis. Increasing W1 emphasizes loss minimization, W2 improves
voltage profile, while W3 and W4 enhance economic and environmental benefits. Their
values are as follows: W1 = 0.4, W2 = 0.25, W3 = 0.1, and W4 = 0.25. These values were chosen
based on the relative importance of minimizing power losses, improving voltage profile by
reducing voltage deviation index, increasing the annual cost of the saved energy losses and
minimizing the annual CO2 emissions. Additionally, several weight combinations were
tested during preliminary simulations, and the selected values provided the best overall
trade-off among the considered objectives.

sections.text:
The combined algorithm used in this work merges the three flowcharts into a single
structured routine. The unified pseudocode is provided below, corresponding to the flow
diagrams. The proposed approach aimed at minimizing the electrical losses, improving the
voltage level on the network buses, verifying economic operation on the network operation
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143262
Energies 2026, 19, 3262 6 of 23
and minimizing the amount of CO2 emissions for improving the environmental condition.
These objectives are connected to each other and can be verified by reducing the current
flows in the network lines. Each line current is dependent on the power flow in this line.
The power flow in any line depends on the loads supplied from this line so, if DGs and
CBs are connected at suitable buses, that will inject both active and reactive power to the
network so the power flow in some lines are reduced and, consequently, the current flows
in these lines are reduced also; then, all objectives are verified.
The proposed Classification-Based Global Optimization (CGO) method is charac-
terized by improving the searching process by including only a small number of buses
from the distribution network; these buses are in the high loaded branches of the radial
distribution network, so the number of iterations needed to obtain the optimal solution
are reduced, and the time consumption for the final solution is minimized, and also the
proposed approach is a cleared systematic method, while other existing methods, such as
PSO, GA, or GWO, rely on stochastic search alone; as mentioned in Table 1, PSO is repre-
sented as black-box optimization technique, GA may give local optima, and Fuzzy Firefly
Algorithm is dependent on a complex tuning of parameters. The results obtained using
CGO in Tables 2–5 show how the performance of the distribution network is improved.
The proposed framework applies classification based on voltage sensitivity and power
demand. These two factors are determined related to the heavily loaded branches of the
network tree, which are known due to the known values of load power on each bus bar in
the network, so there is no probability of working on misclassification.

sections.title: 4 Case Study
sections.text:
To rigorously evaluate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed CGO-based
planning framework, two widely recognized benchmark systems are employed: the IEEE
33-bus and IEEE 69-bus radial distribution networks. These systems are extensively utilized
in distribution system optimization studies due to their well-documented topologies,
realistic load profiles, and characteristic operational challenges. Their adoption enables a
robust assessment of the methodology under varying network scales and complexity levels,
while facilitating direct performance comparison with existing optimization techniques.
The operation in this manuscript is done, assuming only two EVCSs, two CBs and two
DGs because of small distribution networks and for lowering the initial cost of the CBs and
DGs with verifying the objectives of optimal network performance. If the number of units
increases then performance will be improved, but the initial cost will also be increased.
The CGO is an optimization approach that can be applied to any electrical distribution
network. The approach is valid on 33-bus and 69-bus IEEE distribution networks to
demonstrate its effectiveness. Consequently, the proposed approach can be applied on
large real-world distribution networks because the proposed method does not depend on
the network number of buses.
The planning problem for electrical distribution network is done under consideration
of constant load power at each interval, which may be done for daily loading curve with
24 intervals/day, but the EV load is initially assumed to be equal at the beginning of the
approach, but, at the end of the program, the division of this load is at different levels.
The results for capacities of EVCS, DGs and CBs for each EV penetration are tabulated in
Table 6 for 33-bus and in Table 7 for 69-bus distribution networks.

sections.title: 4.1 Base Case of IEEE 33-Bus System
sections.text:
The IEEE 33-bus test system represents a medium-scale radial distribution network
with 33 buses and 32 distribution sections, operating at a base voltage of 12.66 kV and a
base power of 10 MVA. The single-line diagram of the system is presented in Figure 5, with
network parameters, line impedances, and load data sourced from the literature [24–27].
Under base-case conditions—prior to any DG or CB integration—the system exhibits
significant technical inefficiencies, including active power losses of 210.98 kW and reactive
power losses of 143.14 kVAR. These losses, coupled with notable voltage deviations along
the feeder, underscore the need for optimized resource integration to enhance overall
network performance, voltage regulation, and energy efficiency.
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143262
Energies 2026, 19, 3262 14 of 23
Figure 5. IEEE 33-bus distribution system.

sections.title: 4.2 Base Case of IEEE 69-Bus System
sections.text:
To further validate the scalability and robustness of the proposed approach, the
larger IEEE 69-bus distribution network is analyzed. This system comprises 69 buses
and 68 distribution sections, sharing the same base values as the 33-bus system (12.66 kV ,
10 MVA). Its topology and corresponding load data are also obtained from [ 24–27], as
illustrated in Figure 6. In its base configuration, the network experiences active power
losses of 225.0 kW and reactive power losses of 102.13 kVAR. The extended feeder length
and higher number of load points introduce greater voltage drop and loss accumulation,
presenting a more challenging test case for evaluating the optimization methodology’s
ability to maintain voltage stability and minimize losses in larger, more complex networks.
Figure 6. IEEE 69-bus distribution system.
Both test systems serve as representative benchmarks for assessing the efficacy of
the proposed CGO-based planning framework. The progressive increase in network size
from 33 to 69 buses allows for a comprehensive evaluation of the method’s computa-
tional efficiency, solution quality, and practical applicability in real-world distribution
planning scenarios.
